A wage subsidy (lönebidrag) is a form of support that allows an employer to hire you even if your work capacity is reduced for those specific tasks. The support is paid to the employer, not to you, and the decision is made by Arbetsförmedlingen (the Swedish Public Employment Service) after an assessment of what you need at that particular workplace.

## Who the subsidy is for

A wage subsidy exists for you if your work capacity is reduced in relation to a specific job – not because of a diagnosis in itself. That distinction decides everything: Arbetsförmedlingen does not look at what you have, but at what that particular role requires and what you need to manage it. The same person may need the support for one job and not for another.

The assessment is made individually, by a caseworker, usually after talking with you and sometimes in dialogue with the employer about what adjustments would be needed.

## The money goes to the employer, not to you

This is often misunderstood, and it is worth being clear about: the wage subsidy is a contribution toward the employer's wage costs. You receive your salary as usual, on the same terms and under the same collective agreement as other employees. What you might notice is that the employer now has a financial reason why your employment becomes possible, even though the tasks need to be adapted.

This also means the subsidy is tied to the employment and the workplace – not to you as a person forever. If you change jobs, a new assessment has to be made for the new role.

## Who decides, and what is assessed

Arbetsförmedlingen makes the decision, and two things are assessed: whether your work capacity is reduced in relation to the job, and whether the workplace and the tasks are suitable for it. The decision must be in place before the employment starts – so you cannot apply for the subsidy afterward, for a job you already have.

In practice it is often the employer who submits the application, but it is you and your caseworker at Arbetsförmedlingen who lay the groundwork by describing what you need.

## How to bring it up with an employer

This is the hard part. You do not want the wage subsidy to be the first thing an employer hears about you – before she has had a chance to form an opinion about what you can actually do.

A few ways to think about it:

- **Don't wait until the last second, but don't rush either.** Bring it up when the conversation is already about terms of employment – for example, after the employer has shown interest, but before a contract is signed.
- **Describe the adjustment, not the diagnosis.** "I need clear instructions in writing" says more than a diagnosis label, and it is also all the employer needs to know to make the right decision.
- **Explain what the subsidy does for her.** Many employers do not know that wage subsidies exist, or think they are complicated. That you already know how the process works, and that Arbetsförmedlingen handles the assessment, removes some of the uncertainty.
- **Let your caseworker join the conversation if you want.** You do not have to explain everything yourself. The caseworker can contact the employer and describe the process in practical terms.
- **Practice the wording before you say it out loud.** It is easier to find the right tone in advance than in the middle of an interview.

## If your situation changes

A wage subsidy is not a lifelong decision. It is reviewed, and if your work capacity changes – in either direction – the assessment can change with it. It is not a failure if the subsidy is reduced or ends; it is the same mechanism that gave it to you in the first place, now assessing a new situation.

## Frequently asked questions

### Do I have to tell the employer about my diagnosis?

No. What matters to the employer is which adjustments you need, not what causes them. The diagnosis is your own business.

### Can I apply for a wage subsidy myself?

The application is made by the employer, but you are the one who first describes your need to Arbetsförmedlingen. That is why a conversation with your caseworker is the right starting point.

### Does the wage subsidy affect my salary or my terms?

No. You have the same rights, the same collective agreement, and the same salary you would have negotiated anyway. The subsidy only concerns what the employer pays, not what you receive.

## What to do now

Book time with your caseworker at Arbetsförmedlingen and describe concretely what makes certain tasks harder for you – that is the basis the whole assessment is built on. If you want to practice how the conversation with an employer might sound before you are actually in it, that is a good thing to do calmly and in advance, not in the moment.

Read more about the exact terms and current amounts at [arbetsformedlingen.se](https://arbetsformedlingen.se).
summary_en: A wage subsidy goes to the employer, not to you. Here is how the assessment works, and how to bring it up without it becoming the first thing she hears about you.
title_en: Wage subsidy (lönebidrag) – how the support works, and how to bring it up

content_en:
Nystartsjobb (a Swedish wage subsidy for employers) is financial support paid to an employer who hires someone who has been out of the workforce for a long time, or who is newly arrived in Sweden. It is one of the few support schemes built exactly for the situation you might be in.

There is one thing to say right away, because it affects how you should use this text: **you cannot apply for nystartsjobb yourself.** The employer applies for the support. At first this sounds like an obstacle, but it is actually the opposite — it means you have something to offer that you can mention when you apply for jobs. Many small employers do not know this support exists.

The information below comes from the Swedish regulation on support for nystartsjobb (SFS 2018:43) and was checked on 5 August 2026. The rules change often — the regulation has changed at least six times since 2022, most recently with effect from January 2026. Always check with Arbetsförmedlingen (the Swedish Public Employment Service) what applies to you before you plan around anything written here.

## Who can get this support

Whether you qualify depends on how long you have been out of the workforce, measured within what is called a reference period (ramtid).

| Your situation | Time away from work required | Reference period |
|---|---|---|
| 25 years and older | At least 12 months | 15 months |
| 20–24 years | At least 6 months | 9 months |
| Newly arrived immigrant, 20 years and older | Taking part in the introduction programme, or unemployed for at least 6 of the last 9 months. Residence permit granted within the last 36 months | — |
| Participant in the job and development guarantee, 20 years and older | No other qualifying condition required | — |

You also need to be registered as a jobseeker with Arbetsförmedlingen.

The time away from work counts for more than many people think. It includes registered unemployment, labor market programs, sick leave, and unemployment combined with financial assistance (försörjningsstöd). If you were on sick leave for one period and unemployed for another, the time can be added together.

## How long the support can last

The support lasts as long as your time away from work, up to a maximum:

- **25 years and older:** up to 24 months
- **20–24 years:** up to 12 months
- **Newly arrived immigrant:** 24 months if you are 25 or older, 12 months if you are not
- **Job and development guarantee:** 12 months

Decisions are made for a maximum of twelve months at a time, even when the support period is longer than that. This does not mean the employment ends when the support does — the employment can continue longer than the support period.

## What the employer actually receives

The support corresponds to the estimated employer's social security contributions (arbetsgivaravgifter) and the general payroll tax. The amount increases the longer you have been out of work:

- Time away under 24 months: the base level
- Time away 24–36 months: the base level plus an additional amount
- Time away over 36 months, and for newly arrived immigrants: the base level plus 1.5 times the additional amount

Arbetsförmedlingen describes the same scale as one, two, and two and a half times the employer's social security contribution. So a longer time away from work makes the support larger, not smaller.

### About the cap of SEK 20,000

This is the detail that gets repeated incorrectly most often, so it is worth reading slowly.

Only the part of the gross salary that, for full-time work, is **at most SEK 20,000 per month** counts toward the support. For part-time work, the amount is reduced proportionally.

What this does **not** mean:

- It is **not** a cap on what you can earn. Your salary can be higher — that extra part just does not generate more support.
- It is **not** the amount the employer receives. The employer receives an amount corresponding to the contributions, calculated on the part that counts toward the support.

Arbetsförmedlingen has proposed raising the level of the highest wage cost that counts toward the support, but this is a proposal from the agency — not a decision that has been made. SEK 20,000 is what applies today.

## What is required of the employer

This is good to know, partly so you understand why some employers cannot use the support, and partly because it says something about what kind of employment this is:

- The employer must be registered with Skatteverket (the Swedish Tax Agency) and report tax and employer contributions.
- The salary must follow the applicable collective agreement, or at least match the level in the industry.
- The whole salary must be paid electronically into your account throughout the support period. No part may be paid in cash.
- The employer must not have laid anyone off due to lack of work in the last twelve months.

These conditions apply throughout the whole decision period, not just when the application is made.

## How it works, step by step

1. You find an employer who wants to hire you.
2. The employer applies through Mina sidor (My Pages) for employers using e-legitimation (Swedish e-ID). There is a paper application for anyone who cannot use the digital route.
3. The application must be made **at least three weeks before the employment starts**.
4. Once the application has been submitted, a form appears in your activity feed on Mina sidor. There you fill in and confirm your time out of work. A paper form is available here too.
5. You need to be registered with Arbetsförmedlingen when the decision is made. If you have deregistered, you need to register again.
6. The employment can only start once the decision has been made.

Points three and six are connected, and worth saying out loud early in a conversation with an employer: you cannot start on Monday. Plan with a margin.

## What you can say to an employer

You do not need to know the regulation by heart. But since you are the one in the room who knows about the support, it helps to be able to say a few sentences without hesitating:

> "There is a support scheme called nystartsjobb. You, as the employer, apply for it, not me, and it covers the employer's social security contributions for my salary for a period. I meet the conditions. The application is made on your Mina sidor and needs to be sent at least three weeks before I start."

If the employer wants to know more, the information is available on Arbetsförmedlingen's pages for employers. You can also ask your caseworker or consultant for help explaining it — it is a completely normal question to get.

One tip: do not bring up the support as the first thing you say. It works best as an argument once the employer already thinks you seem like a good fit and is wondering whether it can be made to work financially.

## This is a normal job

A nystartsjobb is not an internship and not a program placement. It is a job, with normal employment protection and a salary under the collective agreement. The support is something that happens between the employer and Arbetsförmedlingen — at the workplace, you are a colleague like anyone else.

## Before you move on

The rules above come from the regulation, but your own situation decides what actually applies to you: how your time away from work is counted, how long the support can last, and whether anything has changed since this text was written. Contact Arbetsförmedlingen and ask directly: *"Do I qualify for nystartsjobb, and if so, for how long?"*

This is a question worth asking early. The answer is something you can then carry with you into every conversation with an employer.
summary_en: Everything about nystartsjobb: who can get it, how it works, and how to use it as a door-opener.
title_en: Nystartsjobb — your extra support into working life

content_en:
The cover letter is your chance to show who you are behind the facts in your CV. Here you show your motivation and explain why you are the right fit for the job.

## Why is the cover letter important?

While your CV lists your qualifications, the cover letter explains:
- **Why** you want this specific job
- **How** your experience makes you the right candidate
- **Who** you are as a person and a colleague

A good cover letter can make up for a less impressive CV. On the other hand, a poor letter can ruin the chances of an otherwise strong candidate.

## Structure of the cover letter

### 1. Heading and greeting
- If you know who is recruiting: "Hi Maria!" or "To: Maria Svensson"
- If you don't know: "Hello!" or "To the recruiter in charge"
- Avoid "To whom it may concern" – it is too formal

### 2. Opening – catch interest (2-3 sentences)
The first sentences decide if the recruiter keeps reading. Skip "I am applying for the position of..." – they already know that!

**Weak opening:**
"I am writing to apply for the sales position you advertised on Arbetsförmedlingen (the Swedish Public Employment Service)."

**Good openings:**

*Connection to the company:*
"When I read about your work on sustainable products in Dagens Industri last week, I realized this is a company where my values and experience could really make a difference."

*Personal story:*
"My first contact with programming was when I hacked my sister's computer game at age 12 to get more lives. Since then, I have never stopped solving technical problems."

*Results-focused:*
"During my two years as a customer service representative, I increased customer satisfaction by 23% – and I look forward to doing the same for you."

*Network connection:*
"My former colleague Sara Eriksson told me about your great team and the exciting growth journey you are on, which made me curious to learn more."

### 3. Why this job? (3-4 sentences)
Show that you have done your research about the company:

- What attracts you to this specific company?
- How does this role fit into your career plan?
- What specifically in the job ad caught your interest?

**Example:**
"Your ambition to become the leading company in digital marketing in the Nordic region matches my own drive to stay at the forefront. The Content Manager role is especially interesting because it combines strategic thinking with creative work – exactly the combination I enjoy most."

### 4. Why you? (5-8 sentences)
This is the heart of the letter. Connect 2-3 of your strongest experiences to the job's most important requirements.

**Structure each argument like this:**
1. A requirement from the ad
2. Your relevant experience
3. A concrete result

**Example:**
"You are looking for someone with experience in project management in fast-changing environments. In my current role at TechStart AB, I have led five product launches in 18 months, all delivered on time and within budget. The most recent launch generated 2 million kronor in revenue in the first quarter."

"Your wish for strong communication skills matches my strengths well. As spokesperson for our department, I have given presentations to everyone from boards to external clients, and received consistently positive feedback on my ability to explain complex issues in simple terms."

### 5. Closing (2-3 sentences)
Summarize briefly and show enthusiasm. Include a call to action:

**Example:**
"I am confident that my combination of technical skills and understanding of customers would be valuable to your team. I look forward to telling you more about how I can contribute to your continued success in an interview."

### 6. Closing greeting
- "Med vänliga hälsningar" ("Kind regards" – safe and professional)
- "Vänliga hälsningar" ("Best regards" – a bit less formal)
- "Hör gärna av dig!" ("Feel free to reach out!" – casual, fits startups)

## Example templates: full cover letters

### Template 1: Classic structure (for most jobs)

---

**Hi Sofia!**

When I saw your ad for a Customer Service Representative, I immediately thought this could be a good fit for me. I have followed your company since you launched your app last year, and I am impressed by how you combine technology with a truly personal customer experience.

What attracts me most about this role is the chance to work at the crossing point between technology and human contact. As a natural problem-solver and technology enthusiast, I look forward to helping your customers get the most out of your product.

In my current role at Servicebolaget AB, I handle about 40 customer cases every day by phone and chat. I have consistently received a customer satisfaction score of over 4.8 out of 5, and I have been named "Employee of the Month" three times in the last year. My curiosity about technology means I often help colleagues with more complex IT questions, which I really enjoy.

I am now looking for new challenges at a company where I can grow and develop. Your fast growth and focus on innovation fit perfectly with my ambition, and I believe that my combination of customer service experience and interest in technology would be valuable to your team.

I look forward to telling you more about how I can contribute to your team in an interview.

Kind regards,
Anna Karlsson

---

### Template 2: For career changers

---

**To the hiring manager,**

After ten years in the restaurant industry, I am now taking the step toward a new career in administration – and your Receptionist position has caught my interest.

You might wonder how a cook fits as a receptionist? The restaurant industry has taught me to deliver under pressure, handle many tasks at the same time, and always put the guest's experience first. These skills translate directly into the receptionist role: greeting visitors with a smile, juggling phone calls and bookings, and creating a positive first contact.

During my years as a cook, I have:
- Managed supplier contacts and orders worth millions of kronor every year
- Led a team of 8 people during high-pressure periods
- Learned to always stay calm and professional, no matter the situation

I have recently completed training in the Office suite and administration through Arbetsförmedlingen, where I received the grade VG (Pass with Distinction). My strong work ethic and positive attitude come with me from my previous career.

I am aware that I do not have traditional administrative experience, but I make up for it with enthusiasm for work, adaptability, and a genuine wish to learn. I look forward to the chance to show what I can contribute.

Best regards,
Erik Johansson

---

### Template 3: First job / no experience

---

**Hello!**

I have just finished upper secondary school and I am ready to kick-start my career – and your trainee position in marketing looks like the perfect start.

Even though I do not have formal work experience, I have several relevant achievements. As the person in charge of my school's Instagram for two years, I grew the number of followers from 200 to 2,000, and engagement tripled. I learned everything from content planning to image editing and copywriting – all on my own.

Alongside school, I have:
- Run my own blog about sneakers with 500 unique visitors per month
- Worked part-time in a shop, where I developed my customer communication
- Taken online courses in Google Analytics and Facebook Ads

What drives me is the combination of creativity and data. I love creating content, but I equally love analyzing what actually works. Your emphasis on "data-driven marketing" in the ad fits perfectly with how I think.

I am eager, quick to learn, and ready to give my all. If I get the chance, I promise to exceed your expectations.

Feel free to reach out!
Lisa Andersson

---

## Important principles

✅ **Be personal but professional**
Write the way you talk – just a bit more polished. Let your personality show through.

✅ **Be specific – give examples**
"I am driven" says nothing. "I took the initiative to start a mentorship program that now helps 30 new employees every year" says everything.

✅ **Keep it short (max 1 page)**
300-400 words is ideal. Recruiters do not have time to read novels.

✅ **Adapt it for each job**
At least 50% of the letter should be unique for each application. Generic letters stand out a mile away.

✅ **Start strong**
The first 2-3 sentences decide whether the rest gets read.

✅ **Show, don't tell**
Instead of "I am a good problem-solver" – tell a story about a problem you solved.

## Avoid these mistakes

❌ **Repeating the CV word for word**
The letter should add to the CV, not copy it. Instead, go deeper into the most important points.

❌ **Negative comments about past employers**
"My last boss was incompetent" – This is always wrong, no matter how true it is.

❌ **Language that is too formal or too casual**
"The undersigned hereby requests..." is just as wrong as "Hey! Super cool job!".

❌ **Spelling mistakes and carelessness**
A single spelling mistake can ruin your whole application. Proofread several times.

❌ **Lying or exaggerating**
Anything you write can come up in the interview. Be honest.

❌ **Focusing only on what YOU want**
"I want this job to develop myself" – focus instead on what you can give the company.

❌ **Sending the same letter to everyone**
Recruiters notice right away when a letter is generic.

## Using the AI assistant

If you find it hard to get started, you can use our AI assistant for cover letters. It helps you get a structure to work from.

### How to use AI the right way:
1. **Use AI to brainstorm** – let it suggest openings and structure
2. **Rewrite it in your own voice** – the AI gives you a base, you make it personal
3. **Fill in your own examples** – the AI cannot know your specific experiences
4. **Proofread it critically** – AI can miss nuances and get things wrong
5. **Adapt it for the company** – make sure the letter is really about THIS job

Remember: the AI is a tool, not a replacement for your own voice! Recruiters can often recognize AI-generated text, so make sure the letter really sounds like you.

## Checklist before you send it

- Have I mentioned the company by name?
- Have I connected my experience to the job requirements?
- Do I have concrete examples with results?
- Is the letter under one page?
- Has someone else proofread it?
- Is the tone right for the company and the industry?
- Have I avoided repeating the CV?
- Does the letter end with a clear call to action?
summary_en: Learn how to write a cover letter that grabs interest and shows why you are the right person for the job.
title_en: Cover Letter – Your Chance to Stand Out

An internship (praktik) is one of the most effective ways to gain experience and build a network, and it often leads to a job. Here is how to do it.

The big advantage of an internship is that it flips the burden of proof. In a normal job application, you have to convince someone about what you can do based on a piece of paper. In an internship, they get to see it directly — and for someone with gaps in their CV or who is changing industries, it is often a much shorter path in.

## Types of internships

### Work trial (arbetsprövning)
- Arranged through Arbetsförmedlingen (the Swedish Public Employment Service)
- You keep your benefit payments
- Purpose: to test whether the job is a good fit

### Internship through school or training
- Often part of the training program
- Gives you course credits
- LIA (workplace-based learning)

### Volunteer internship
- Non-profit organizations
- Gives you experience and references
- Often more flexible

### Self-arranged internship
- You take the initiative yourself
- Contact companies directly
- Can be for shorter periods

Which type suits you depends mostly on whether you need to keep receiving benefits during the internship. If you receive benefits from Arbetsförmedlingen or Försäkringskassan (the Swedish Social Insurance Agency), always check with your caseworker **before** you say yes to anything. The rules differ between different types of benefits, and it is easier to ask in advance than to sort it out afterward.

## Benefits of an internship

✅ **Gain experience to put on your CV**
✅ **Build a network**
✅ **Test whether the job suits you**
✅ **Show what you can really do**
✅ **A possible path to a job**

## How to find internship placements

1. **Arbetsförmedlingen** – ask about a work trial
2. **Your school** – talk to a study counselor
3. **Contact companies directly** – send a speculative application
4. **Praktikplatser.se** and similar websites
5. **Your network** – ask friends and family

What works best for most people is point three, even though it feels the hardest. Most internship placements are never advertised — they happen when someone asks. Smaller employers say yes more often than large ones, because they can decide on their own without going through an HR process.

## How to ask a company directly

Keep it short. A five-line email gets more replies than a twenty-line one.

Write who you are, what you want to learn, how long and how many days a week, and what it means for them in practice. If you have benefit payments that continue during the internship, say so. The fact that the internship will not cost them any wages is often the detail that makes the decision.

Consider calling a few days later. Many people say yes on the phone who would never have replied to the email.

## How to apply for an internship

### In your application, emphasize:
- Your motivation to learn
- What you want to achieve
- What you can offer (even if it is basic)
- That you are reliable and committed

### During the internship:
- **Be curious and ask questions**
- **Take initiative** – ask "can I help with...?"
- **Be on time and reliable**
- **Network** – get to know people
- **Keep a record** of what you do, for your CV

The point about keeping a record is the one people forget, and it costs the most. Write down every week which tasks you did and which systems you used. After ten weeks, you will have material for both your CV and interview answers — if you try to remember it afterward, all you will have is "I did an internship."

## Turn the internship into a job

1. **Ask for a closing conversation** with your supervisor
2. **Ask for a reference** or a letter of recommendation
3. **Ask whether there is a chance of being hired**
4. **Stay in touch** after the internship

Do not wait until the last week to ask about a job. Bring it up around the halfway point: "If there is a need going forward, I am very interested — what would I need to show before then?" This way you get both an answer and a chance to live up to it.

Ask for the reference while they still remember you well, and save your supervisor's phone number and email before you finish.

## If the internship is not what you expected

It is okay to stop if:
- You are not learning anything
- The environment is harmful
- You are being taken advantage of

Talk to your supervisor or Arbetsförmedlingen.

One warning sign worth knowing about: an internship should give you learning, not replace a paid employee. If you are doing the same work as the staff, alone and without supervision, week after week, it is no longer an internship. Bring this up with your caseworker.

## Remember

An internship is an investment in yourself. Even if it does not lead directly to a job, you gain valuable experience and contacts!
summary_en: How to find, apply for, and get the most out of an internship to get your foot in the door.
title_en: Internships as a path into working life

Trial employment (provanställning) is often the first step into a new workplace. Here you will learn how it works, what rights you have, and what you can expect.

## What is a trial employment?

A trial employment is a time-limited employment where both you and the employer get the chance to try out whether it works. It is a period for both sides to assess whether it is the right match.

### Basic rules
- **Maximum length:** 6 months (can be shorter under a collective agreement)
- **Written agreement:** Must always be documented
- **Automatically converts:** Into permanent employment after the trial period if no one ends it

## Your rights during trial employment

### The same basic rights
During a trial employment you have, in principle, the same rights as other employees:
- The right to pay under the agreement
- The right to vacation (which you earn over time)
- The right to sick pay
- Protection against discrimination
- The right to a safe working environment
- The right to parental leave

### What is different
- **Shorter notice period:** Often 14 days or none at all
- **Easier to end:** The employer does not need to give a valid reason
- **No seniority protection:** You do not have the same protection if there are layoffs due to lack of work

## What happens during the trial employment?

### The employer's responsibility
- Give you a proper introduction
- Explain what is expected
- Give you a real chance to succeed
- Give you feedback on your work
- Tell you in time if the employment will not continue

### Your responsibility
- Do your best
- Ask for help when you need it
- Take feedback on board
- Show commitment and willingness to learn
- Follow the rules of the workplace

## Tips for succeeding during your trial employment

### The first few weeks
1. **Listen actively** – Understand the company's culture and way of working
2. **Ask questions** – This is expected and appreciated
3. **Keep notes** – Write down what you learn
4. **Be on time** – Show that you take the job seriously
5. **Be positive** – Attitude matters a lot

### Throughout the period
- **Ask for regular feedback** – Ask how things are going
- **Show initiative** – Be proactive without going outside your role
- **Build relationships** – Get to know your colleagues
- **Document your progress** – Note what you learn and achieve
- **Communicate** – Say something if you are struggling with anything

### Toward the end of the trial employment
- Book a meeting with your manager 2-3 weeks before it ends
- Ask directly: "How do you see my employment going forward?"
- Ask for concrete feedback
- Discuss future goals and development

## If the trial employment ends

### If the employer does not want to continue it
The employer must inform you at least 14 days before the trial employment ends. If they miss this, you may be entitled to compensation.

**Important:** The employer does not need to give a reason, but they may not end it for discriminatory reasons.

### If you do not want to continue
You also have the right to end the trial employment. Follow the agreed notice period.

### What you can do
1. **Ask for an explanation** – You have the right to ask why (even though they do not have to tell you)
2. **Ask for a written reference** – Good to have for future applications
3. **Be professional** – Do not burn any bridges
4. **Learn from the experience** – What could you do differently next time?

## When the trial employment becomes permanent

### What changes?
- You get full protection against dismissal
- You are covered by seniority rules
- The notice period becomes longer
- You have the right to know the reason if you are dismissed

### What you should do
- Ask for written confirmation of the new type of employment
- Discuss any salary adjustment
- Talk about development opportunities
- Review your insurance

## Common questions

**Can a trial employment be extended?**
No, not under the law. It can be a maximum of 6 months in total.

**What happens if I get sick?**
You have the right to sick pay. However, the trial employment can still be ended.

**Can I take vacation?**
You earn vacation days but usually cannot take them during a short trial employment.

**Can I lose the job for any reason at all?**
Almost — but not for discriminatory reasons (for example, pregnancy, disability, or ethnic background).

## Checklist: Trial employment

**Before you start:**
- [ ] Read and understood the employment contract
- [ ] Know when the trial employment starts and ends
- [ ] Understand what goals are expected

**During the period:**
- [ ] Documenting my progress
- [ ] Asking for feedback regularly
- [ ] Showing commitment and initiative

**Toward the end:**
- [ ] Booked a meeting with the manager
- [ ] Asked about continued employment
- [ ] Discussed future development

## Remember

Trial employment is not only a test of you — it is also a chance for you to assess the workplace. Does the job suit you? Do you get along with your colleagues? Do you see a future here? Your feelings and observations matter just as much as the employer's.
summary_en: A guide to the rules of trial employment, your rights, and what happens afterward.
title_en: How trial employment works — everything you need to know

A reference check is often the last step before a job offer. It's your chance to have others confirm the picture you have given of yourself. Here you'll learn how to prepare yourself and your references.

## What is a reference check?

A reference check is when a potential employer contacts people you have named to get a picture of you as an employee. It's usually done:
- After the interview(s), before a decision is made
- By phone (most common) or email
- For 15-30 minutes per reference
- With 2-3 references

## Who can be a reference?

### Good references
- **Former managers** – Best choice, they can assess your work performance
- **Project managers** – If you have worked on projects
- **Colleagues** – Can talk about how you work with others
- **Clients/partners** – An outside perspective
- **Supervisors** – From an internship or thesis project

### Not ideal as references
- Family members
- Close friends (unless the relationship is work-related)
- People who haven't seen your work
- People you have had a conflict with

### If you don't have any work references
If you have just graduated or have been away from the job market:
- Teachers or supervisors
- Internship supervisors
- Club or association leaders
- Volunteer coordinators
- Fellow students (for group projects)

## How to choose the right references

### Things to consider
1. **Relevance** – Can they speak to what the job requires?
2. **Relationship** – How well do they know your work?
3. **Time** – How long ago did you work together?
4. **Attitude** – Will they speak well of you?
5. **Availability** – Can they take a call?

### Vary your references
Try to have a mix of:
- Different types of relationships (manager, colleague)
- Different workplaces
- Different time periods
- Different skill areas

## Prepare your references

### Before you give out their names
**Always ask first!** Contact your reference and:
1. Ask if they have the time and are willing
2. Explain which job you have applied for
3. Tell them what the role involves
4. Discuss what you'd like them to highlight
5. Give them relevant information

### Information to share with your reference
- The job ad or role description
- Your CV (updated)
- What you emphasized in the interview
- Which qualities matter for the job
- Roughly when they can expect a call

### Template for contacting a reference

**Subject:** Can you be a reference for me?

"Hi [Name],

I'm currently applying for a position as [title] at [company], and I've come far in the process. They now want to contact references, and I thought of you right away.

The role is about [short description], and they are looking for someone who is [qualities]. I have highlighted my experience with [relevant things] and how we worked together on [specific project/task].

Would you be able to be my reference? They will likely call within [timeframe].

Thank you in advance!
[Your name]"

## What do employers ask about?

### Common questions in a reference check

**About the working relationship:**
- "How do you know [name]?"
- "How long, and in what capacity, did you work together?"
- "What was [name]'s role and responsibilities?"

**About work performance:**
- "How would you describe [name]'s work performance?"
- "What were [name]'s main strengths?"
- "Are there areas where [name] could improve?"

**About collaboration:**
- "How did [name] work within the team?"
- "How did [name] handle stressful situations?"
- "How was [name]'s communication with colleagues and clients?"

**About leadership (if relevant):**
- "How did [name] lead their team?"
- "How did [name] handle conflicts?"

**Closing questions:**
- "Would you hire [name] again?"
- "Is there anything else we should know?"

### What they really want to know
- Does this match the picture the candidate gave?
- Are there any warning signs?
- Is this person a good fit for this specific role?
- How will this person work out with us?

## What happens after the reference check?

### Positive signs
- They call back the same day or the day after
- They want to discuss practical details
- They ask about your notice period
- They mention the next step

### Silence or rejection
- If you haven't heard anything in a week, follow up
- Ask if they need more information
- A rejection doesn't necessarily have anything to do with the references

## If something goes wrong

### If a reference says something negative
- You may never find out exactly what was said
- Ask the reference for honest feedback
- Consider replacing that reference

### If the employer can't reach your reference
- Always keep contact details up to date
- Have backup references ready
- Let your references know when a call might come

### If you suspect a reference isn't speaking well of you
- You can hire a company that checks your references for you
- Replace references you're unsure about
- Be honest about difficult relationships in the interview

## Checklist: Reference check

**Before you apply:**
- [ ] Identified 3-4 potential references
- [ ] Asked if they are willing to be a reference
- [ ] Collected accurate contact details

**When you've come far in the process:**
- [ ] Told your references about the specific job
- [ ] Sent relevant information
- [ ] Confirmed they can be reached

**After the reference check:**
- [ ] Thanked your references
- [ ] Told them how it went
- [ ] Updated them on the outcome

## Remember

Your references are part of your professional network. Treat them well, stay in touch even between job searches, and be ready to be a reference for them too. A strong network of people who can vouch for your skills is valuable throughout your entire career.

**Tip:** Always thank your references afterward, whether or not you got the job. A short email or text message is enough!
summary_en: Everything you need to know about reference checks: how to choose your references, prepare them, and what employers actually ask.
title_en: Reference Checks – What Happens and How to Prepare

You have sent in your application. Then nothing visible happens – and it is easy to think that means no. Usually, it just means you cannot see the process going on behind the scenes. Here are the steps, what matters at each one, and why silence rarely means the answer you fear.

## Step 1: Screening – before a human reads your application

Many recruitment processes, especially at larger employers or through recruitment companies, start with automatic screening. A system reads through the applications and sorts them based on set requirements – often basic requirements like education, language, or years of experience, rather than a nuanced review. This is why it is worth using the wording from the job ad in your application: the system looks for matching text, not for your own best way of saying the same thing.

What gets stopped here is often stopped for technical reasons – the wrong file format, a key skill missing from the text even though you actually have it, or a CV that is hard to read structurally. This rarely says anything about you as a person.

## Step 2: Selection – who reads on, and why

The applications that pass screening are read by a person – a hiring manager, HR, or a recruitment consultant. Here, it is about the whole picture: does your experience match, does the cover letter feel well thought out, is there anything that stands out in a good way. This is also where references to specific results or responsibilities make a difference, because it is hard to judge on anything other than what is actually written there.

## Step 3: First contact

Often a short phone call, sometimes an email with a few questions. The purpose is rarely to test you – it is to confirm basic things: are you still interested, does your salary expectation roughly match, when can you start. Answer honestly and briefly. This is not the interview, even if it can feel like a small screening call.

## Step 4: Interview rounds

Most processes have between one and three rounds of interviews. What is assessed differs:

- **The first interview** usually covers a basic match – experience, motivation, how you communicate.
- **The second interview** often goes deeper, sometimes with another person in the room – a future colleague or the manager's manager. Here, they test how you think about real situations, not just what you have done before.
- **A possible third round** is more often about checking details and overall fit – by this point, it is already between a small number of candidates.

## Step 5: Tests or a work sample

Not every process has this step, but more do now than before. It can be an aptitude test, a personality test, or a practical task. Read more about what the different tests measure and how to prepare in our guide on work psychology tests.

## Step 6: Checking references

References are usually checked late, once the employer has already decided that you are the one they want to move forward with – it is a confirming step, not a screening step. This is why checking references often feels like a good sign, and it usually is.

## Step 7: The offer

Last comes the actual offer – role, terms, start date. At this point, it is reasonable to ask questions and ask for time to think before you answer. If you receive an offer verbally, always ask to get it in writing before you accept it for real.

## Why silence between the steps rarely means no

This is the most common source of unnecessary worry in the whole process. Between each step above, there are internal things happening that you never see: the manager is on vacation, the budget needs internal approval, another candidate needs to finish their interviews first, or HR is running several processes at once and yours is just one of them. None of this has anything to do with your performance.

An actual no almost always comes as a clear message – an email or a call, even if sometimes a short one. In practice, silence usually just means the process is taking longer than you expected, not that it is over. That does not make the waiting easier, but it is worth remembering before you draw a conclusion you do not have evidence for.

## What should I do now

If you have waited a long time with no response, the next step is not to guess – it is to ask. Read our guide on following up on your application to learn how to do that without seeming pushy. Keep track of where each application is in the process, so you know when it is actually the right time to reach out.

## Frequently asked questions

### How do I know which step I am at if no one has told me?
Ask the recruiter directly after an interview: "What is the next step, and roughly when can I expect to hear something?" Most people are happy to answer – it is a natural question to end the conversation with.

### Does it mean anything extra if checking references takes a long time?
Not necessarily. References can be hard to reach, may be traveling, or may need several reminders. This says more about their schedule than about you as a candidate.

### Can I skip a step if I have already done something similar before, for example a work sample at another employer?
You can ask, but expect no. Every employer assesses candidates based on their own process and their own criteria, even if the task looks similar on the surface.
summary_en: Screening, selection, interviews, tests, references, and the offer – what matters at each step, and why silence in between rarely means no.
title_en: The recruitment process, step by step

Rusta och matcha (a job-coaching service arranged through Arbetsförmedlingen, the Swedish Public Employment Service) is the most common way to get extra support in your job search, but few people know that they actually choose who gives them that support, and can switch if it does not work out. Here is what the service is, how you choose, and what to do if something feels wrong.

## What Rusta och matcha is

Rusta och matcha is a service that Arbetsförmedlingen can offer you if you need extra support to move forward toward a job or studies. Instead of Arbetsförmedlingen coaching you directly, you are connected to an independent provider, a company approved by Arbetsförmedlingen to deliver this specific service. The support period is time-limited and can be extended if there are reasons for it based on your situation in the labor market.

## You choose the provider yourself, and you can switch

This is the part most people miss: you choose which provider you want, in a similar way to how you choose a health center. Arbetsförmedlingen shows you the providers available in your area, but the decision is yours. If it does not work out — because the fit is not right, because the provider does not give you what you need, or for any other reason — you have the right to switch to a different provider. You do not need a legally valid reason. It is enough that the support is not working for you.

## What a provider actually has to deliver

A provider within Rusta och matcha must give you individually adapted support toward a job or studies, not a generic course where everyone gets the same version. In practice, this usually means:

- An initial meeting where you go through your situation, your goals, and what you need help with.
- Regular check-ins during the support period.
- Concrete help with job searching, such as your CV, applications, and contact with employers, adapted to what you specifically need.
- A final meeting where you go through together what has happened and what the next step is.

What the provider must deliver in detail is described in Arbetsförmedlingen's assignment to the providers. Ask the provider to show you what is included if you are unsure.

## Questions to ask before you choose

Before you decide, ask the provider:

- How often do we meet, and is it in person, online, or both?
- What experience do you have with my industry or situation?
- What happens if I am not satisfied — is there a way to raise that before I switch?
- Who is my contact person, and what do I do if that person is not available?

A good answer is concrete. A weak answer is vague and avoids details.

## When the cooperation is not working

If you notice after a while that it is not giving you anything — meetings that feel empty, no progress, poor contact — you do not have to put up with it until the support period ends. Contact your caseworker at Arbetsförmedlingen and ask to switch provider. Be specific about what has not worked. This makes switching easier and helps Arbetsförmedlingen keep track of which providers are doing a good job.

## Who decides what, and where you check what currently applies

Arbetsförmedlingen decides whether you are entitled to Rusta och matcha and which providers are approved in your area. The provider does not decide your benefits or your status as a job seeker — that stays with Arbetsförmedlingen and, where relevant, your a-kassa (unemployment insurance fund) or Försäkringskassan (the Swedish Social Insurance Agency). You can see which providers are available where you live, and how to switch, by logging in to [Arbetsförmedlingen's](https://arbetsformedlingen.se) Mina sidor (My Pages).

## Rusta och matcha does not replace your activity report

Even if you have a provider supporting you every week, you remain a job seeker with Arbetsförmedlingen, with everything that involves. You still need to submit your activity report on time, and you still need to keep up contact with your a-kassa or Försäkringskassan if you receive benefits based on that. The provider can help you keep track of what you have done, but the responsibility for reporting stays with you. Do not mix up your meetings with the provider with the obligations you have directly toward Arbetsförmedlingen.

## What to do now

If you have been offered Rusta och matcha, compare a few providers in your area before you choose, and ask the questions above. If you already have a provider that is not working: contact your caseworker at Arbetsförmedlingen and request a switch. You do not need an approved reason.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does it cost anything to switch providers?
No, it is free for you as a job seeker. Providers are paid by Arbetsförmedlingen, not by you.

### Can I decline Rusta och matcha entirely?
That depends on your situation and what is written in your plan of action. Talk to your caseworker about what applies to you.

### Does switching providers affect my benefits?
Switching by itself does not affect your benefits. What can affect it is if you do not take part in the support at all, regardless of provider.
summary_en: What Rusta och matcha is, that you choose your own provider, what questions to ask, and what to do when it does not work out.
title_en: Rusta och matcha — How to Choose a Provider, and How to Switch

SIUS stands for "särskilt introduktions- och uppföljningsstöd" (special introduction and follow-up support), and it means a person – a SIUS consultant – who helps you settle into a new job and stays on as support for a while after you start. This support is available both before and after your employment begins, not just at a single point in time.

## What a SIUS consultant does

A SIUS consultant is trained in introduction methods and works in a hands-on way, often out at the workplace together with you. It is not about meetings in an office – it is about being there, where the work actually happens.

In practice, it can look like this:

- The consultant learns the tasks together with you, sometimes by doing them alongside you for a period.
- The consultant breaks down unclear steps into parts that are easier to learn.
- The consultant acts as a link between you and your manager, especially early on, when no one is quite sure how much needs explaining.
- The consultant reduces their presence gradually as you become more confident in the role, instead of disappearing all at once.

## The support covers the whole transition

Many people think SIUS is only about the first few days on a job. That is not the case. The support is made up of two connected parts:

**Introduction support** comes first – the consultant is there and helps you learn the tasks together with you, often closely during the first few weeks.

**Follow-up support** comes afterward, once you are already employed. The consultant checks in, follows up on how things are going, and is available if something needs to be sorted out – with you or with the employer.

The fact that the support continues after you start the job is the part that usually comes as a surprise, and the part that makes a difference when a new job feels fragile in the first few months.

## How you become eligible for SIUS

You need to be registered as a job seeker with Arbetsförmedlingen (the Swedish Public Employment Service) and have a need for extra support to get established at a workplace – a need that your case officer assesses together with you. It is not something you order in advance yourself; it grows out of the conversation about what it would take for a job to work for you.

Good times to bring it up:

- When you and your case officer talk about why previous jobs or internships did not work out.
- When an employer has shown interest but is unsure what the employment would require from them.
- When you feel that it is not the tasks themselves that are difficult, but everything around them – understanding what is expected, finding routines, daring to ask questions.

## What you can ask the consultant for, in concrete terms

It is easy to assume the support is vague or general. It is not. You can ask for things like:

- **Coming along to a job interview**, as support, or to explain what support is available to the employer.
- **Explaining a specific work task** in a way that works for you, if the normal introduction goes too fast or is unclear.
- **Talking to your manager** about what is difficult right now, if you cannot find the words yourself in the moment.
- **Being there the first few days**, if it is the newness of everything – a new place, new people, new routines – that is the hard part.

The more clearly you can describe what usually causes trouble, the easier it is for the consultant to give you the right support at the right moment.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does SIUS cost me anything?
No. The support is free for you and is arranged through Arbetsförmedlingen.

### Will the employer know why I have a SIUS consultant?
What you choose to share is up to you. You and the consultant agree together on how much needs to be explained to the employer – often it is enough to say which adjustments are needed, not why.

### What happens if it still does not work out at that workplace?
Then it is something you and the consultant talk through together. A workplace not being the right fit is not a failure in itself – it is information that carries over into the next attempt.

## What should you do now

Bring up SIUS with your case officer at Arbetsförmedlingen, ideally before a job starts rather than after it already feels difficult. Describe as concretely as you can what usually tends to be hard in the transition to a new job – that is the basis for what support you are offered.

More about how to become eligible is available at [arbetsformedlingen.se](https://arbetsformedlingen.se).
summary_en: A SIUS consultant helps you settle into a new job, both before and after you start. Here is how you become eligible, and how you can use the support in practice.
title_en: SIUS – Support When You Are Starting a New Job

Getting sick, or needing to stay home with a sick child, can feel extra uncertain when you have just started a new job. Here is who pays, in what order, and who you should actually call.

## Step one: you report sick to your employer, not to an authority

If you get sick, the first step is always to tell your employer, as soon as you can, following the routines that apply at your workplace. You do not contact Försäkringskassan (the Swedish Social Insurance Agency) at this stage – they come in later, if the period of sick leave continues for a while.

## Who pays when you are sick, and in what order

Responsibility shifts in two steps:

| Who | What applies |
|---|---|
| Your employer | Pays sick pay during an initial period of sick leave, with a qualifying deduction at the start of the period |
| Försäkringskassan | Takes over and pays sickness benefit if the period of sick leave continues longer than the period your employer is responsible for |

You do not need to keep track of exactly when responsibility shifts over – that is handled between your employer and Försäkringskassan. Your task is to report sick on time and hand in the certificates that are requested once the period of sick leave has gone on for a while.

If you are employed by the hour, or do not have the right to sick pay from an employer for other reasons, Försäkringskassan handles the whole calculation instead, including the qualifying deduction, from the first day.

## What is the qualifying deduction, and why does it exist

The qualifying deduction (karensavdrag) is a part of your sick pay that is deducted at the start of a period of sick leave, no matter what time of day you get sick or what your schedule looks like. The idea behind it is that sick leave should carry a small cost for the employee too, not only for the employer – it is a rule set out in law, not something your employer has made up.

**One thing worth knowing:** if you get sick again shortly after being back at work, it is often counted as a continuation of the same period of sick leave rather than a new one, and then no new qualifying deduction is made. Exactly where the line is can depend on whether the workplace has a collective agreement – ask your employer or your union if you are unsure in a specific situation.

## When is a medical certificate required

For the first days of a period of sick leave, it is normally enough to report that you are sick yourself, without a certificate. If the period of sick leave continues, a medical certificate is required, both for your employer to continue paying sick pay and later for Försäkringskassan to pay sickness benefit. Exactly when the certificate is required can differ depending on whether the workplace has a collective agreement that changes the usual limit – ask your manager or HR if you are unsure, instead of guessing.

## VAB – caring for a sick child

VAB, "vård av barn" (care of a child), is the compensation you can apply for when you need to stay home to take care of a sick child instead of going to work. It is called temporary parental benefit and is paid by Försäkringskassan, not by your employer.

Two things to keep separate:

- **You report VAB to Försäkringskassan** – that is where the application for compensation goes.
- **You tell your employer separately** that you are absent, just as with your own illness, so they know you will not be coming in.

If the period of VAB continues for a while, Försäkringskassan can ask for a certificate to confirm that the child still needs care, in the same way as with your own illness.

## Who do you call, and when

A quick rule of thumb:

- **You are sick, at the start of the period** → tell your employer.
- **You are sick, and it continues for a while** → Försäkringskassan takes over, often automatically based on your employer's report, but make sure you have handed in the certificates that are required.
- **Your child is sick** → apply for VAB with Försäkringskassan, and tell your employer that you are away.
- **Unsure about the qualifying deduction, certificate deadlines, or what applies to your employment** → ask your employer, Försäkringskassan, or your union. No one expects you to know this by heart when you are new.

[forsakringskassan.se](https://www.forsakringskassan.se)

## What to do now

Find out what applies for reporting sick at your workplace before you need to use it – who you call, and whether there is an app or system for it. Save Försäkringskassan's contact details somewhere easy to find. And do not feel strange about asking your manager directly how the qualifying deduction or medical certificates work – it is a question everyone who is new to a job has.

## Frequently asked questions

### Do I need to have worked for a certain time before I get sick pay?
Sick pay is linked to being employed, not primarily to how long you have worked. There are exceptions for very short employments – if you are unsure, ask your employer or your union about your specific situation.

### What happens if I get sick during my probationary period?
The same rules apply as for other employment – being on probation does not change your right to sick pay.

### Can I take VAB for children other than my own?
In some cases, for example if you are the one who actually cares for the child day to day even if you are not the legal guardian. If your situation is not the usual family picture, check with Försäkringskassan what applies to you.
summary_en: Who pays when you are sick or caring for a sick child, what the qualifying deduction (karensavdrag) is, when a medical certificate is required, and who to call.
title_en: Sick Pay, the Qualifying Deduction, and VAB – When You Are New to a Job

Registering with Arbetsförmedlingen (the Swedish Public Employment Service) is the first practical step when you become a job seeker, and timing matters. Here is when to do it, what happens during registration, and how to prepare for your first meeting.

## Why the first day matters

Register with Arbetsförmedlingen on your first day without work — not the week after, and not once you've "had time to think it through." The reason is that several things connected to your benefits are counted from your registration date, not from the day you actually became unemployed. If you wait, everything that depends on being registered waits too: your contact with a caseworker, your action plan, and the documentation your a-kassa (Swedish unemployment insurance fund) or Försäkringskassan (the Swedish Social Insurance Agency) needs to assess your benefits.

## How registration works

Registration is done digitally, logged in with an e-identification on Arbetsförmedlingen's website. You fill in information about your education, your work experience, your skills, and what kind of job you're looking for. At the end of the process, you book a time for your first meeting with a caseworker. If you don't have an e-identification, or need help with the technology, support is available. Contact Arbetsförmedlingen to find out how this can be arranged for your situation.

## The planning meeting — what it is

The planning meeting is your first real meeting with a caseworker, either digitally or in person depending on what's offered where you live. You go through your background, what you're aiming for, and what support might be right for you. The result is an individual action plan: a document describing your goals, what you need to do to reach them, and how often you need to report your activity. The action plan isn't fixed — it's updated as your situation changes, so let your caseworker know if something no longer applies.

## Being registered is not the same as participating in a program

This is often misunderstood. Being registered as a job seeker means you're on record with Arbetsförmedlingen and have an action plan — it's a basic status. Participating in a program, for example Rusta och matcha (a job-matching program) or a labor market training course, is a separate decision on top of that, which Arbetsförmedlingen makes based on what you need. So you can be registered without taking part in any program, but you cannot take part in a program without first being registered.

## How to prepare for your first meeting

Know these things before the meeting, so it goes faster and you get more out of it:

- **Your CV**, even if it isn't finished — a draft is enough.
- A list of **your education and past jobs**, with approximate time periods.
- What you **want to work with**, or which industries you're open to, if you're not sure.
- If you have a **disability or a health condition** that affects what support you need, it's good to mention it here, since it determines what support you can be offered.
- Any questions you already have, written down so you don't forget them in the moment.

## What happens after registration

Registration isn't a one-time step but a status you need to keep active. As soon as you're registered, Arbetsförmedlingen's routines start running: you need to submit an activity report regularly, you may be assigned to a program or support such as Rusta och matcha if your caseworker decides you need it, and your action plan needs to be followed up and updated whenever something changes in your situation. If you receive benefits from your a-kassa or activity support through Försäkringskassan, continued payment depends on you keeping up with these parts, not just on having registered once. If your situation changes — a new job, illness, moving — let Arbetsförmedlingen know so your status stays accurate.

## What should you do now

If you're unemployed today and not registered: do it now, not tomorrow, on [Arbetsförmedlingen's](https://arbetsformedlingen.se) website. If you already have a planning meeting booked: gather the items from the list above before you go in, so you can get further in less time.

## Frequently asked questions

### Do I need to register even if I'm about to start a new job soon?
If you know you won't need support, you can choose to deregister again within a short period after signing up, and you won't need a planning meeting. If you're unsure, register anyway. There's no cost to having the status if you don't end up needing it.

### What happens if I miss my planning meeting?
Contact Arbetsförmedlingen as soon as possible to reschedule. A missed meeting without an explanation can affect how your situation is assessed later on.

### Can I change caseworkers if it doesn't feel right?
Yes, you can ask to switch. Contact Arbetsförmedlingen's customer service or your current caseworker and explain why.
summary_en: When to register, what happens during registration, what the planning meeting is, and how to prepare.
title_en: Registering With Arbetsförmedlingen – How It Works

The dream of starting your own business appeals to many people. But entrepreneurship is not for everyone, and it is good to know that before you take the step. This guide helps you evaluate if self-employment is right for you.

## Is Entrepreneurship Right for You?

### It May Suit You If You...
- Are comfortable with uncertainty and change
- Are self-motivated without outside structure
- Have a high tolerance for risk
- Can handle financial uncertainty
- Are good at making decisions
- Like doing many different kinds of tasks
- Are willing to work hard (at the start)

### It May Not Suit You If You...
- Need security and predictability
- Do not like making decisions alone
- Want a clear line between work and free time
- Prefer to focus on one task
- Struggle with financial stress
- Need outside motivation

### Questions to Ask Yourself
1. What is driving me to want to start my own business?
2. Do I have a business idea that solves a real problem?
3. Is there a market for my service/product?
4. Do I have a financial buffer for 6–12 months?
5. Does my family/partner support the decision?
6. What is my plan B if it does not work out?

## Types of Business

### Sole Trader (Enskild Firma)
**The simplest form**
- Easy to start (online in 15 minutes)
- You and the business are the same legal person
- You are personally responsible for debts
- For tax purposes, it is part of your personal finances
- Good for testing an idea and low-risk business

### Limited Company (Aktiebolag, AB)
**Most common for growth**
- A separate legal person
- Limited personal liability
- Requires 25,000 SEK in share capital
- More administration (bookkeeping, annual report)
- Better if you plan to bring in investors or hire staff

### Trading Partnership (Handelsbolag)
**For two or more people**
- Partners are jointly liable
- A flexible structure
- Suits simple partnerships

### Economic Association (Ekonomisk Förening)
**For cooperatives**
- Owned by its members
- At least 3 members
- Democratic governance

## Before You Start

### 1. Test Your Idea
- Are there customers willing to pay?
- Test it with real customers (not friends)
- Run a small pilot before you go all in
- Research: Do similar services exist? How are they doing?

### 2. Make a Business Plan
A simple plan is enough:
- What are you selling?
- Who to?
- How do you reach them?
- What does it cost to run?
- How do you make money?
- What is your goal for the first year?

### 3. Financial Preparation
- How much do you need to earn?
- How long can you go without income?
- What are the start-up costs?
- Do you need funding?

### 4. Practical Preparation
- A business name and domain
- A business bank account
- Insurance
- A bookkeeping system
- Any required permits

## Funding

### Your Own Money
- Safest option
- No debt
- You keep control
- Limits your potential

### Loans
- A bank loan (requires collateral)
- A microloan (for example, from ALMI)
- A private loan

### Support and Grants
- A start-up grant through Arbetsförmedlingen (the Swedish Public Employment Service)
- Innovation support
- EU grants
- Municipal support

### Investors
- Angel investors
- Venture capital
- They provide capital in exchange for a share of ownership

## Common Challenges

### Financial Uncertainty
- Uneven income
- Late payments
- High costs at the start
- **Solution:** A buffer and a realistic budget

### Loneliness
- No colleagues to talk things through with
- Hard to stay motivated
- Every decision rests on you
- **Solution:** Networking, mentors, coworking spaces

### Work-Life Balance
- Work takes over
- Hard to switch off
- Family and relationships are affected
- **Solution:** Set boundaries, plan time off

### Sales and Marketing
- You have to sell yourself
- A constant search for new customers
- Marketing costs time and money
- **Solution:** Build on referrals, learn digital marketing

### Administration
- Bookkeeping, VAT, taxes
- Contracts and legal matters
- Takes time away from your core work
- **Solution:** Automate tasks, hire help

## Alternatives to Working Full-Time

### Start on the Side
- Keep your job
- Test on a small scale
- Build up slowly
- Reduce the risk

### Freelance/Consulting
- Sell your skills by the hour
- Lower risk than a product business
- Flexibility
- Built on your expertise

### Franchise
- A proven concept
- Support from the franchise owner
- Less freedom but lower risk

### Buy an Existing Business
- Already has customers and income
- Requires capital
- A careful risk analysis is important

## Resources and Support

### Advice
- **ALMI:** Advice and funding
- **Nyföretagarcentrum:** Free advice
- **Drivhuset:** For students and young people
- **Coompanion:** Cooperatives and associations

### Networking
- Local business networks
- Industry organizations
- Coworking spaces
- Business groups on LinkedIn/Facebook

### Education
- Start-your-own-business courses (Arbetsförmedlingen, komvux [municipal adult education])
- Business courses
- Industry-specific knowledge

## Checklist: Starting Your Own Business

**Before deciding:**
- [ ] Evaluated if it suits you
- [ ] Tested the idea with potential customers
- [ ] Made a simple business plan
- [ ] Mapped out the finances

**When starting:**
- [ ] Chosen a business type
- [ ] Registered the business
- [ ] Opened a business account
- [ ] Arranged insurance
- [ ] Set up bookkeeping

**The first months:**
- [ ] Got your first customer
- [ ] Set up simple routines
- [ ] Built a network
- [ ] Made adjustments based on what you have learned

## Summary

Starting your own business can be very rewarding – and challenging. The key is to go in with open eyes, prepare well, and be ready to learn along the way. Start small if you can, test your idea, and build from there. If it is not right for you right now, that is also a valuable insight – employment suits many people better, and there is nothing wrong with that.
summary_en: An honest guide to starting a business: advantages, challenges, and how to decide if entrepreneurship is right for you.
title_en: Starting Your Own Business – Is It for You?

Job searching is one of the more stressful experiences in life. Here are tools to help you manage the stress.

One thing is worth saying right away: the stress you feel is not a sign that you are doing something wrong. Job searching includes almost everything research points to as stressful — uncertainty, repeated rejections, financial worry, and a lack of control over the outcome. Feeling bad about it is a reasonable reaction to an unreasonable situation.

## Understand Your Stress

### Do You Recognize These Signs?

**Physical:** Trouble sleeping, headaches, tiredness
**Mental:** Worry that will not stop, trouble concentrating
**Behavioral:** Avoidance, procrastination

These are normal reactions.

Avoidance usually does the most damage, because it builds on itself. You put off an application, feel guilty, and the guilt makes the next application even harder to start. If you recognize that spiral: it is broken by doing one small thing, not by deciding to do everything at once.

## Managing Stress in the Moment

**4-7-8 breathing:**
1. Breathe in for 4 seconds
2. Hold for 7 seconds
3. Breathe out for 8 seconds

**The 5-4-3-2-1 technique:**
Name 5 things you can see, 4 you can feel, 3 you can hear, 2 you can smell, and 1 you can taste.

**Physical movement:**
Go for a walk – even 5 minutes helps!

These techniques do not make the problem smaller. They lower your body's alarm level so that you can think clearly again. That is the whole point — you do not need to feel calm, you just need to get back to a level where you can make a decision.

## When Worry Comes at Night

Worrying at night is especially common when you are job searching, because that is when your brain finally has quiet around it. Two things usually help:

**Write it down.** Keep paper by your bed. Worry that is written down does not need to be held in your head until morning.

**Set a worry time during the day.** Fifteen minutes, the same time every day, when you deliberately let yourself worry. It sounds strange, but it works for many people: when worry comes at other times, you can tell yourself it can wait until your worry time.

## Managing Stress in the Long Term

### Structure Creates Security
- Set routines
- Clear limits on job searching

Set an end time for job searching each day, and stick to it. Without a limit, job searching becomes something that runs in the back of your mind around the clock, and then you get neither real rest nor effective work — just a bad conscience all the time.

### Physical Health
- Prioritize sleep (7–9 hours)
- Move for 30 minutes a day
- Eat regularly

If 30 minutes feels impossible: take ten. What you can actually manage on a bad day is worth more than something that only works on a good day.

### Mental Strategies
- Challenge negative thought patterns
- Try mindfulness or meditation
- Keep a journal

Challenging a thought does not mean thinking positively. It means checking if the thought is actually true. "I will never get a job" is a prediction, not a fact. Ask yourself what you actually know, and what you just feel.

### Social Support
- Talk about it
- Ask for help

Unemployment is isolating, and isolation makes stress worse. Seeing someone once a week is not a luxury — it is part of what helps you cope.

## When You Should Seek More Help

Self-care is not always enough, and that is not a failure. Seek care if you recognize any of the following:

- Feeling down or anxious for most of the day, for more than two weeks
- Your sleep is not working even though you have tried changing your routines
- You are withdrawing from people you care about
- You use alcohol or other substances to cope
- You have thoughts of harming yourself

Contact your local health center, or call **1177** for medical advice, available 24 hours a day. If you have urgent thoughts of suicide: call **112**, or **Mind's Suicide Hotline at 90101**.

Getting help for how you feel does not hurt your job search. It usually makes it easier.

## Remember

You are not your productivity. It is okay to rest. You can get through this – one day at a time.
summary_en: Practical techniques for managing stress and worry during your job search.
title_en: Stress Management for Job Seekers
